M04:D3.2.teach: EXPLAIN is a causal chain, not merely a verdict. For one-dimensional motion with a>0, signed velocity increases. If v starts negative, its magnitude decreases until v=0; after v becomes positive its magnitude increases. The speed minimum follows from the sign change, not a reversal of acceleration. At v=0 the acceleration may remain nonzero. If acceleration is switched to zero at the zero-velocity event, the body remains at rest under that new condition. State each link and its warrant: acceleration controls signed velocity change; speed is magnitude; zero crossing changes which sign branch defines the magnitude.

M05:D3.2.teach: A velocity change acquired early affects more of the subsequent position history than the same change acquired late. For example, two carts start at 2 m/s; one increases speed by 3 m/s early, then coasts, while the other acquires the same increase later. Their final speeds agree because their signed acceleration areas agree. The early cart carries its extra velocity for longer; its v–t area is larger, hence it has larger displacement. If the same change is a reduction, the ordering reverses. This is the missing causal bridge between a–t and x–t.

M08:D3.2.teach: At constant nonzero circular speed, a rim marker's tangent rotates. Equal magnitudes do not make successive vectors equal: subtract nearby tangents to obtain a small inward-directed change (toward the midpoint radius, then toward the instantaneous centre in the small-time limit). Since acceleration is the rate of vector change, it is nonzero despite constant speed. After a complete revolution the velocity vector returns to its initial value, so its full-lap average acceleration is zero. A straight constant-velocity comparison isolates direction change as the reason.

M05:D4.7.teach: Swapping two acceleration stages changes when velocity is acquired. For durations p,q and rates a,b, the endpoint velocity u+ap+bq is invariant. For the first ordering, x_X=up+ap²/2+(u+ap)q+bq²/2; reverse ordering yields x_Y=uq+bq²/2+(u+bq)p+ap²/2. Thus x_X−x_Y=(a−b)pq. This exact warrant says nothing by itself about total distance: |v| must be integrated separately when signs differ. A reversal-free nonnegative condition licenses distance=displacement; without it, construct opposite-direction equal-path examples.

M06:D4.7.teach: In the two-stage braking model with shared initial u and total T, switch time τ and switch speed w, distance=(uτ+wT)/2. Half reference distance is equivalent to w=u(1−τ/T); both segment slopes then equal −u/T. This is a valid converse only with exactly two linear segments and nonnegative velocity. With three intervals the same total area can be achieved by unequal slopes: complementary speeds v(t)+v(T−t)=u guarantee half-area. An explicit counterexample tests why the model restriction is necessary.
